hook_text: In 1840 a six-year-old could sit alone in a coal mine for twelve hours in total darkness. His job was to open a door.
clip_script: A six-year-old sits in a pitch-black tunnel deep underground. He is a trapper. When a coal tub rumbles towards him, he pulls open a wooden door, then shuts it to keep air flowing through the mine. Twelve hours. Alone. In the dark. Older children crawl through tunnels too low to stand in, dragging tubs of coal with chains round their waists. Up in the cotton mills, eight-year-olds piece broken threads and crawl under machines that are still running. Fourteen-hour days, fines for lateness, straps for falling asleep. Why? Children were cheap and their families needed every penny. Then evidence changed everything. Parliament heard children's own stories. Drawings from the mines shocked the country. The laws came step by step: 1833, no children under nine in the mills; 1842, no women, girls or young boys underground; 1847, a ten-hour day.
visual_style: A whiteboard mine tunnel with a tiny figure beside a trapdoor and a lamp flickering out; then a mill floor with a child under a moving machine; then a timeline with 1833, 1842 and 1847 stamping onto it.
pacing: A slow, still opening in the dark, rising pace through the mill, then firm beats on each law.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and see how evidence changed the law.
